title: Causal identification of the avian magnetic receptor
open: Which molecule and which cellular pathway actually make a bird's magnetic compass work — that is, can we identify the receptor whose perturbation abolishes magnetic compass behavior and whose restoration rescues it?
status: The problem has been investigated for decades. Cryptochrome 4 from the European robin shows magnetic sensitivity in vitro [Xu et al. (2021), "Magnetic sensitivity of cryptochrome 4 from a migratory songbird," DOI: 10.1038/s41586-021-03618-9], but in vitro sensitivity alone does not establish its causal role in a living bird. The leading hypothesis is the radical-pair mechanism [Hore and Mouritsen (2016), "The Radical-Pair Mechanism of Magnetoreception," DOI: 10.1146/annurev-biophys-032116-094545].
solved_when: A causal chain is demonstrated in a living bird: a molecular perturbation of the candidate receptor eliminates magnetic compass behavior, and restoring that receptor restores the behavior — establishing necessity and sufficiency.
why: It would settle a major unsolved sensory mechanism in biology and could guide the design of artificial chemical sensors.
key_works: Xu et al. (2021), “Magnetic sensitivity of cryptochrome 4 from a migratory songbird,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-021-03618-9); Hore and Mouritsen (2016), “The Radical-Pair Mechanism of Magnetoreception,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-biophys-032116-094545).

title: Anatomical identification of a magnetite-based receptor
open: Is there a sensory organ in any animal whose magnetite crystals demonstrably transduce magnetic-field information into nerve signals? Success would require a reproducibly identifiable magnetite-containing structure whose mechanics, innervation, and experimental perturbation together establish magnetic transduction rather than ordinary iron storage.
status: The proposed iron-rich receptors in the pigeon beak were shown in 2012 by Treiber et al. to be macrophages rather than magnetosensitive neurons. This correction does not rule out all magnetite-based mechanisms, but a causally validated receptor remains missing.
solved_when: A magnetite-containing sensory structure is reproducibly identified and causally linked to magnetic sensing — its biophysics, innervation, and response to perturbation shown to support magnetic transduction rather than iron-storage function.
why: It would distinguish between competing mechanisms of animal magnetic sensing and anchor magnetite-based magnetoreception in anatomy rather than correlation.
key_works: Treiber et al. (2012), “Clusters of iron-rich cells in the upper beak of pigeons are macrophages not magnetosensitive neurons,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature11046).

title: Traceable magnetic-hyperthermia power measurements
open: Can the community establish reference magnetic nanoparticles and interlaboratory measurement protocols such that calorimetric and magnetic determinations of heating power agree, with full field, mass, and heat-loss uncertainty budgets?
status: The RADIOMAG consortium published recommendations in 2021 (Wells et al., "Challenges and recommendations for magnetic hyperthermia characterization measurements," DOI: https://doi.org/10.1080/02656736.2021.1892837); routine comparability across instruments and biologically relevant conditions remains a practical target.
solved_when: Certified reference particles exist and a documented interlaboratory protocol yields statistically consistent calorimetric and magnetic power measurements, including complete uncertainty accounting for field amplitude, sample mass, and heat-loss corrections.
why: Without traceable measurements, comparisons of particle designs and heating experiments across labs are not defensible, stalling progress in magnetic nanomedicine.
key_works: Wells et al. (2021), “Challenges and recommendations for magnetic hyperthermia characterization measurements,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1080/02656736.2021.1892837).

title: Quantitative human-scale magnetic particle imaging
open: Can magnetic particle imaging be made quantitative at human scale — that is, can it recover absolute tracer concentration, not just relative signal, in human-sized anatomy? Formally, this asks for a system meeting defined resolution, frame-rate, heating, stimulation, and calibration requirements across realistic tracer environments.
status: Human-scale construction is established; a 2025 brain-imaging prototype reported approximately 5–7 mm phantom resolution, per Mattingly et al. (2025), "Design, construction and validation of a magnetic particle imaging (MPI) system for human brain imaging," [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1088/1361-6560/ad9db0). Quantitative in-vivo transfer remains more demanding. The foundational technique traces to Gleich and Weizenecker (2005), "Tomographic imaging using the nonlinear response of magnetic particles," [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature03808).
solved_when: A human-scale MPI system recovers absolute tracer concentration in human-sized anatomy while meeting the defined resolution, frame-rate, heating, stimulation, and calibration requirements across realistic tracer environments.
why: Achieving this enables traceable particle tracking and image-guided interventions.
key_works: Gleich and Weizenecker (2005), “Tomographic imaging using the nonlinear response of magnetic particles,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature03808); Mattingly et al. (2025), “Design, construction and validation of a magnetic particle imaging (MPI) system for human brain imaging,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1088/1361-6560/ad9db0).

title: Fluctuating trimerons above the Verwey transition
open: Do the trimeron-like electronic units that order below magnetite's Verwey transition survive as fluctuating, localized objects above it — and if so, what are their populations, lifetimes, and mutual interactions? A quantitative description of this dynamical high-temperature state should explain the observed transport and structural behavior across doping and temperature.
status: The transition itself dates to 1939, and the low-temperature charge/orbital/trimeron structure was resolved in major detail in 2012; the dynamical high-temperature state remains unresolved. Key works: Senn, Wright, and Attfield (2012), "Charge order and three-site distortions in the Verwey structure of magnetite," [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature10704); Attfield (2022), "Magnetism and the Trimeron Bond," [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.chemmater.2c00275).
solved_when: A validated account of the populations, lifetimes, and interactions of localized electronic units above the Verwey transition exists and explains transport and structural properties across doping and temperature ranges.
why: It would clarify how electronic, lattice, and magnetic ordering couple in mixed-valence oxides, resolving the long-standing dynamical side of the Verwey problem.
key_works: Senn, Wright, and Attfield (2012), “Charge order and three-site distortions in the Verwey structure of magnetite,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature10704); Attfield (2022), “Magnetism and the Trimeron Bond,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.chemmater.2c00275).

title: Dating the magnetization of Hadean zircons
open: When did individual magnetic inclusions in Hadean zircons acquire their remanent magnetization, independently of the crystallization age of their host zircons?
status: Studies report Hadean magnetic signals, including supporting analyses in 2020, e.g. Tarduno et al. (2020), "Paleomagnetism indicates that primary magnetite in zircon records a strong Hadean geodynamo," [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1916553117). However, pervasive later remagnetization has been documented by Weiss et al. (2015), "Pervasive remagnetization of detrital zircon host rocks in the Jack Hills, Western Australia and implications for records of the early geodynamo," [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.epsl.2015.07.067), so alteration and remagnetization must be tested inclusion by inclusion.
solved_when: The timing of remanence acquisition is determined inclusion by inclusion, with later alteration and remagnetization ruled out, reconciling the conflicting interpretations of the earliest geodynamo record.
why: The answer constrains early core evolution and Earth's surface environment in the Hadean.
key_works: Tarduno et al. (2020), “Paleomagnetism indicates that primary magnetite in zircon records a strong Hadean geodynamo,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1916553117); Weiss et al. title: Unambiguous identification of ancient magnetofossils
open: Can we tell biogenic magnetite or greigite apart from abiotic look-alikes in ancient rocks, given that dissolution, recrystallization, chain collapse, and aging may have erased or distorted the original signals? The goal is a set of independently testable, multimodal identification criteria that hold under every preservation history.
status: Morphology, microscopy, and FORC central ridges provide evidence of a biological origin, but no single magnetic signature proves it under every preservation history. Heslop et al. (2014), "Characterizing magnetofossils from first-order reversal curve (FORC) central ridge signatures," [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/2014GC005291); Roberts et al. (2011), "Magnetic properties of sedimentary greigite (Fe3S4): An update," [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1029/2010RG000336).
solved_when: A set of multimodal criteria exists that unambiguously distinguishes biogenic magnetite or greigite from abiotic look-alikes after dissolution, recrystallization, chain collapse, and aging, with each criterion independently testable.
why: It would make reconstructions of ancient microbial ecosystems defensible rather than suggestive, since current evidence cannot rule out abiotic false positives.
key_works: Heslop et al. (2014), “Characterizing magnetofossils from first-order reversal curve (FORC) central ridge signatures,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/2014GC005291); Roberts et al. (2011), “Magnetic properties of sedimentary greigite (Fe3S4): An update,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1029/2010RG000336).

title: Haldane gap for the spin-1 Heisenberg chain
open: Does the antiferromagnetic spin-1 Heisenberg chain have a strictly positive spectral gap in the thermodynamic limit? Formally: prove that the translation-invariant, nearest-neighbor antiferromagnetic spin-1 Heisenberg chain with periodic boundaries has a spectral gap bounded below by a positive constant independent of chain length.
status: Proposed in 1983, the conjecture has extensive numerical and experimental support. The rigorous gap known for the AKLT chain does not settle the Heisenberg case because the Hamiltonians differ. Haldane (1983), "Nonlinear Field Theory of Large-Spin Heisenberg Antiferromagnets," [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.50.1153); Affleck et al. (1987), "Rigorous Results on Valence-Bond Ground States in Antiferromagnets," [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.59.799).
solved_when: A rigorous proof establishes a strictly positive lower bound on the spectral gap, uniform in the chain length, for the translation-invariant, nearest-neighbor antiferromagnetic spin-1 Heisenberg chain with periodic boundaries.
why: It establishes the foundational distinction between integer-spin and half-integer-spin quantum magnets, the central claim of the Haldane conjecture.
key_works: Haldane (1983), “Nonlinear Field Theory of Large-Spin Heisenberg Antiferromagnets,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.50.1153); Affleck et al. (1987), “Rigorous Results on Valence-Bond Ground States in Antiferromagnets,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.59.799).

title: Low-spin honeycomb XY order
open: Does the nearest-neighbor spin-1/2 XY antiferromagnet on the honeycomb lattice exhibit ground-state long-range order? A proof should settle this case and extend to the other low-spin cases that remain unresolved.
status: Wojtkiewicz, Wohlfeld, and Oleś (2023), “Long-range order in the XY model on the honeycomb lattice,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.107.064409), proved honeycomb ordering for spin at least 2 in 2023. The rigorous bound does not reach the low-spin cases supported by spin-wave calculations.
solved_when: A rigorous proof establishes ground-state long-range order for the nearest-neighbor honeycomb XY magnet at spin 1/2, and the argument covers the remaining unresolved low-spin values.
why: It probes exactly how low coordination and strong quantum fluctuations limit existing ordering proofs, sharpening the boundary between what spin-wave theory predicts and what can be rigorously established.
key_works: Wojtkiewicz, Wohlfeld, and Oleś (2023), “Long-range order in the XY model on the honeycomb lattice,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.107.064409).

title: Positive-temperature quantum Heisenberg ferromagnetism
open: Does the nearest-neighbor quantum Heisenberg ferromagnet on the three-dimensional cubic lattice — particularly in the spin-1/2 case — exhibit spontaneous magnetization at sufficiently low positive temperature? In other words, one seeks a proof that a nonzero spontaneous magnetization persists at low but strictly positive temperature in this canonical model.
status: This is a longstanding mathematical-physics problem. Rigorous low-temperature free-energy asymptotics are known to agree with spin-wave theory — as established by Correggi, Giuliani, and Seiringer (2015), "Validity of the spin-wave approximation for the free energy of the Heisenberg ferromagnet," [arXiv:1312.7873](https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.7873), following the problem statement of Lieb (1999), "Long Range Order for the Quantum Heisenberg Model," [problem statement](https://web.math.princeton.edu/~aizenman/OpenProblems_MathPhys/9901.HeisenbergFerr.html) — but these results do not establish spontaneous magnetization.
solved_when: A rigorous proof of spontaneous magnetization at sufficiently low positive temperature for the nearest-neighbor quantum Heisenberg ferromagnet on the three-dimensional cubic lattice, in particular for spin 1/2.
why: It supplies the missing rigorous explanation of the simplest quantum ferromagnet, closing a foundational gap in the theory of magnetic order.
key_works: Lieb (1999), “Long Range Order for the Quantum Heisenberg Model,” [problem statement](https://web.math.princeton.edu/~aizenman/OpenProblems_MathPhys/9901.HeisenbergFerr.html); Correggi, Giuliani, and Seiringer (2015), “Validity of the spin-wave approximation for the free energy of the Heisenberg ferromagnet,” [arXiv:1312.7873](https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.7873).

title: Mass generation in the two-dimensional classical Heisenberg magnet
open: Does the nearest-neighbor two-dimensional classical Heisenberg (O(3)) magnet develop a mass gap at every positive temperature? A proof would show exponential decay of correlations at all positive temperatures, and would further establish the low-temperature asymptotics of the correlation length.
status: The field-theory prediction dates to 1975. Aru, Garban, and Sepúlveda’s 2025 work, “Percolation for 2D Classical Heisenberg Model and Exit Sets of Vector Valued GFF” ([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00220-024-05208-y)), resolves parts of competing geometric arguments without proving the full lattice mass-gap statement.
solved_when: Exponential decay of correlations is proven at every positive temperature in the nearest-neighbor two-dimensional O(3) model, together with the low-temperature correlation-length asymptotics.
why: It connects an elementary magnet to the phenomenon of nonperturbative mass generation, the same mechanism at the heart of the Yang–Mills mass gap.
key_works: Aru, Garban, and Sepúlveda (2025), “Percolation for 2D Classical Heisenberg Model and Exit Sets of Vector Valued GFF,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00220-024-05208-y).

title: Square-lattice J1–J2 intermediate phase
open: Does the spin-1/2 square-lattice J1–J2 antiferromagnet host a genuine spin-liquid phase between its Néel and valence-bond-ordered regimes? More precisely, is there a finite spin-liquid region in the parameter space, and if so, what are its boundaries and its gap?
status: The problem has been studied since the 1980s. Numerical methods disagree over whether a narrow liquid region exists, over plaquette versus columnar order, and over finite-size extrapolation; DMRG supports plaquette order in part of the nonmagnetic regime. Key work: Gong et al. (2014), "Plaquette Ordered Phase and Quantum Phase Diagram in the Spin-1/2 J1–J2 Square Heisenberg Model," [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.113.027201).
solved_when: The existence (or absence) of a finite spin-liquid region between Néel and valence-bond order is established, along with its boundaries and gap.
why: It settles whether the nonmagnetic regime contains a stable spin liquid or is merely a broad crossover between ordered phases.
key_works: Gong et al. (2014), “Plaquette Ordered Phase and Quantum Phase Diagram in the Spin-1/2 J1–J2 Square Heisenberg Model,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.113.027201).

title: Triangular J1–J2 spin-liquid universality
open: Is the intermediate phase of the triangular spin-1/2 J1–J2 Heisenberg model a stable gapless Dirac spin liquid, a gapped spin liquid, or some other phase — and if so, what are its universal observables? More precisely, one wants a controlled identification of the phase and its universal properties that survives the thermodynamic limit.
status: DMRG established a strong spin-liquid candidate in 2015 [Zhu and White (2015), “Spin liquid phase of the S=1/2 J1–J2 Heisenberg model on the triangular lattice,” arXiv:1502.04831]. Recent dynamical calculations support Dirac descriptions [Willsher and Knolle (2025; revised 2026), “Dynamics and stability of U(1) spin liquids beyond mean-field theory: Triangular-lattice J1–J2 Heisenberg model,” arXiv:2503.13831], but finite-cylinder and approximation dependence remain unresolved.
solved_when: The nature of the intermediate phase (Dirac liquid, gapped liquid, or other) is established, together with its universal observables, with the conclusion robust to finite-cylinder effects and approximation dependence.
why: A settled characterization yields quantitative predictions for triangular-lattice magnetic materials.
key_works: Zhu and White (2015), “Spin liquid phase of the S=1/2 J1–J2 Heisenberg model on the triangular lattice,” [arXiv:1502.04831](https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.04831); Willsher and Knolle (2025; revised 2026), “Dynamics and stability of U(1) spin liquids beyond mean-field theory: Triangular-lattice J1–J2 Heisenberg model,” [arXiv:2503.13831](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.13831).

title: Spin-1/2 pyrochlore Heisenberg ground-state selection
open: What is the true ground state of the nearest-neighbor spin-1/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnet on the pyrochlore lattice, and what excitations does it support? In the thermodynamic limit, the problem is to determine whether the system selects a valence-bond crystal, a quantum spin liquid, or something else, and to characterize the resulting excitation spectrum.
status: Unsettled after roughly three decades. A 2025 unrestricted variational study — Cheng and Li (2025), "Closely competing valence bond crystal orders in the ground state of the spin-1/2 antiferromagnetic Heisenberg model on the pyrochlore lattice…," [arXiv:2509.13746](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.13746) (title abbreviated) — finds nearly degenerate, structurally distinct crystals selected by tiny further-neighbor exchanges.
solved_when: The infinite-system ground-state phase is identified — with the nature of its (possibly valence-bond-crystal or liquid) order established — and its excitation spectrum is determined.
why: It establishes what three-dimensional geometric frustration alone produces, anchoring our understanding of how competing interactions in frustrated magnets give rise to exotic order.
key_works: Cheng and Li (2025), “Closely competing valence bond crystal orders in the ground state of the spin-1/2 antiferromagnetic Heisenberg model on the pyrochlore lattice…” [arXiv:2509.13746](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.13746), title abbreviated.

open: What is the true ground state of the spin-1/2 nearest-neighbor Heisenberg antiferromagnet on the hyperkagome lattice — a gapless liquid, a gapped topological liquid, or valence-bond order — and what are its low-temperature thermodynamics?

title: Honeycomb Néel-to-plaquette transition
open: Does the spin-1/2 honeycomb J1–J2 model lose its Néel order through a continuous deconfined transition, a weak first-order transition, or an intervening phase as frustration is increased?
status: Numerical and coupled-cluster studies since 2011 identify nearby plaquette order, including Farnell et al. (2011), “Frustrated Heisenberg antiferromagnet on the honeycomb lattice: A candidate for deconfined quantum criticality,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.84.012403). Small order parameters and long crossover scales obstruct an asymptotic diagnosis.
solved_when: A controlled asymptotic determination of the nature of the transition out of the Néel phase — deconfined continuous, weakly first-order, or via an intermediate phase — is established for the spin-1/2 honeycomb J1–J2 model.
why: It tests how lattice symmetry and monopoles shape unconventional criticality, informing broader questions of conformal fixed-point existence and confinement transitions in lattice gauge theories.

title: Intrinsic versus disorder-generated liquid behavior in YbMgGaO4
open: Which low-energy signatures of YbMgGaO4 survive once the Mg/Ga exchange randomness is removed, and does the idealized material Hamiltonian itself support a quantum spin liquid?

title: Random transverse fields in Pr2Zr2O7
subfield: Spin ice and three-dimensional emergent electrodynamics
open: Can a U(1) quantum spin liquid in Pr2Zr2O7 survive the random strain and transverse fields present in real samples, or does that disorder inevitably freeze it into a glass or quadrupolar state at the lowest energies? Formally, this asks whether disorder permits a coherent Coulomb phase in the low-energy limit or drives a transition to a non-liquid ground state.
status: Two 2017 studies established the importance of random strain in Pr2Zr2O7 and proposed different disorder-mediated pictures: Wen et al. (2017), "Disordered Route to the Coulomb Quantum Spin Liquid: Random Transverse Fields on Spin Ice in Pr2Zr2O7" ([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.118.107206)), and Martin et al. (2017), "Disorder and Quantum spin ice" ([arXiv:1708.01845](https://arxiv.org/abs/1708.01845)). A common quantitative defect-to-phase theory remains incomplete.
solved_when: A theory (or equally rigorous numerics/analysis) yields a definite answer: either a demonstration that a coherent U(1) liquid persists at the lowest energies under random strain and transverse fields, or a proof of instability to a glass or quadrupolar state — ideally in the form of a common quantitative defect-to-phase framework.
why: It determines whether disorder is a help or a hindrance to emergent electrodynamics: if randomness can stabilize rather than destroy the Coulomb phase, disordered materials become a route to spin-liquid physics rather than an obstacle to it.

title: Continuous ferromagnetic quantum criticality in clean metals

title: Pure-state organization of the three-dimensional Edwards–Anderson glass
open: Does the short-range three-dimensional Ising spin glass, in the thermodynamic limit, possess many pure states organized by a nontrivial overlap structure, or only a pair of spin-flip-related states with trivial overlaps? Modern simulations find nontrivial overlaps, while Vedula, Moore, and Sharma (2025), "Nature of spin glass order in physical dimensions," [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevE.111.034102), argue that some apparent replica-symmetry-breaking signatures can arise from finite-size droplets.
solved_when: The thermodynamic pure-state structure and overlap distribution of the three-dimensional Edwards–Anderson Ising spin glass are rigorously or convincingly determined, with the droplet, replica-symmetry-breaking, and intermediate scenarios definitively distinguished.
why: It settles which features of mean-field glass theory survive in physical magnets, determining the organizing physics of real disordered systems.
key_works: Fisher and Huse (1986), “Ordered Phase of Short-Range Ising Spin-Glasses,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.56.1601); Vedula, Moore, and Sharma (2025), “Nature of spin glass order in physical dimensions,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevE.111.034102).

why: The answer decides whether an applied field destroys or merely modifies the equilibrium glass phase, settling whether mean-field replica symmetry breaking applies to real-dimensional spin glasses.

status: Multiple limiting descriptions are individually successful, but a transferable theory identifying where local temperatures fail or where mode-selective transport dominates remains open; see Bauer, Saitoh, and van Wees (2012), “Spin caloritronics,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/nmat3301).
solved_when: A predictive theory reproduces spin-Seebeck signals across temperature, thickness, frequency, and interfaces using independently determined electron, magnon, phonon, and boundary parameters, and identifies regimes where local-temperature descriptions fail or mode-selective transport dominates.
why: It would enable rational design of thermally driven spin currents rather than case-by-case fitting, and would pinpoint where the widely used local-temperature picture breaks down.
key_works: Bauer, Saitoh, and van Wees (2012), “Spin caloritronics,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/nmat3301).

title: Parameter-predictive ultrafast demagnetization theory
open: Can ultrafast demagnetization be predicted as a function of material, thickness, excitation, and interface properties using only inputs determined independently of the demagnetization measurement itself? In other words, is there a theory whose quantitative predictions are transferable without retuned phenomenological rates?
status: Since the 1996 nickel experiment of Beaurepaire et al. (1996), "Ultrafast Spin Dynamics in Ferromagnetic Nickel," [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.76.4250), several mechanisms — including superdiffusive spin transport as described by Battiato et al. (2010), "Superdiffusive Spin Transport as a Mechanism of Ultrafast Demagnetization," [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.105.027203) — have been shown to explain important regimes. However, the quantitative partition among these mechanisms, and the transferability of their parameters across systems, remain unresolved.
solved_when: A single theory, with no fitted relaxation times or retuned phenomenological rates, quantitatively predicts demagnetization across materials, thicknesses, excitation conditions, and interfaces, with all inputs independently constrained.
why: It would convert empirical ultrafast optimization into predictive design, replacing trial-and-error tuning of laser and sample parameters with a priori material selection.
key_works: Beaurepaire et al. (1996), “Ultrafast Spin Dynamics in Ferromagnetic Nickel,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.76.4250); Battiato et al. (2010), “Superdiffusive Spin Transport as a Mechanism of Ultrafast Demagnetization,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.105.027203).

title: Rare-earth-free optically written tunnel-junction memory
open: Can a rare-earth-free magnetic material be integrated into a tunnel-junction memory cell that is written by single optical pulses while still meeting practical device requirements? Specifically, can single-pulse all-optical switching be combined with useful tunneling contrast, adequate retention, low error rates, and process compatibility across a broad fluence and temperature window?
status: Gadolinium-free Mn2RuxGa toggle switching was demonstrated in 2020 [Banerjee et al. (2020), "Single pulse all-optical toggle switching of magnetization without gadolinium in the ferrimagnet Mn2RuxGa," DOI: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-020-18340-9]. The joint memory-cell requirements — combining this switching with tunnel-junction functionality — remain unresolved.
solved_when: A rare-earth-free material exhibiting single-pulse optical switching is demonstrated as a tunnel-junction memory cell simultaneously satisfying useful tunneling contrast, retention, low error rates, and process compatibility over a broad fluence and temperature window.
why: It would free optical memory from dependence on rare-earth (e.g., gadolinium-based) materials, broadening both the palette of usable magnetic materials and the security of supply chains for these devices.
key_works: Banerjee et al. (2020), “Single pulse all-optical toggle switching of magnetization without gadolinium in the ferrimagnet Mn2RuxGa,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-020-18340-9).

title: Sustained gigahertz all-optical magnetic writing
open: Can an all-optical magnetic memory sustain independently chosen writes at gigahertz rates? That is, demonstrate long sequences of arbitrary writes while measuring error rates, retention, endurance, and steady-state thermal control.

(2021), "Dual-shot dynamics and ultimate frequency of all-optical magnetic recording on GdFeCo," [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41377-020-00451-z).
solved_when: A demonstration shows sustained gigahertz-rate sequences of independently chosen writes, with measured write errors, data retention, endurance, and steady-state thermal behavior under that operation.
why: It determines whether ultrafast all-optical switching translates into sustained device throughput rather than isolated fast events.
key_works: Wang et al. (2021), “Dual-shot dynamics and ultimate frequency of all-optical magnetic recording on GdFeCo,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41377-020-00451-z).

title: Low-heating, lasting optical reprogramming of exchange
open: Can light reversibly reprogram the exchange interaction or magnetic order of a material so that the change persists beyond the pulse, while keeping unwanted heating bounded and clearly distinguishing coherent control from mere thermal alteration?
status: Theory was advanced in 2015 by Mentink, Balzer, and Eckstein (2015), "Ultrafast and reversible control of the exchange interaction in Mott insulators," [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms7708); light-driven-phonon control was demonstrated in 2021 by Afanasiev et al. (2021), "Ultrafast control of magnetic interactions via light-driven phonons," [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41563-021-00922-7). Durable, efficient repeated programming remains open. Related directions include prethermal Floquet states and nonlinear phononics without excess heating.
solved_when: A demonstration achieves durable, efficient, repeated optical programming of exchange or magnetic order — persistent beyond the pulse duration — with bounded unwanted heating and a clear separation of coherent control from thermal effects.
why: It would enable magnetic functions that are unavailable through static magnetic fields, opening routes to ultrafast, repeatable control of magnetic interactions.

title: Fast nondestructive electrical readout of nanoscale skyrmions

Scaled high-bandwidth operation remains unresolved.
solved_when: A demonstrated electrical readout identifies one small skyrmion at useful latency with calibrated signal-to-noise ratio, energy cost, and disturbance to the texture, and separates occupancy detection from size-fluctuation sensitivity.
why: It is the missing link that lets skyrmion-based storage and logic talk to conventional electronic circuits; without a fast, nondestructive electrical signal, skyrmion devices cannot be integrated with mainstream electronics.

solved_when: A working system demonstrates task scaling and generalization across independently fabricated arrays, with the total energy budget — initialization, training, instrumentation, and readout — quantified, and with scalable advantage over suitable baselines.
why: It tests whether many-body magnetic dynamics offer practical computation rather than a laboratory curiosity, determining whether these reservoirs can compete with conventional computing baselines.

title: Wafer-scale ambient-stable room-temperature ultrathin magnets
subfield: Two-dimensional and van der Waals magnetic devices
open: Can atomically thin magnets be grown as uniform wafers that actually survive the fab — films that keep working at room temperature, in air, through a full device process?

why: Practical atomically thin magnetic building blocks would let 2D spintronic and magnetic devices move from lab demonstrations to manufacturable technology.

title: Integrated exciton–magnon magnetic photonics
subfield: Two-dimensional and van der Waals magnetic devices
open: Can an integrated optical modulator or coherent processing element be built on exciton–magnon coupling in a van der Waals magnet, and does the coupling survive device patterning? The goal is a working component with measured loss, modulation depth, bandwidth, and drive energy.

solved_when: A functioning integrated optical modulator or coherent processing element is demonstrated, with reported loss, modulation depth, bandwidth, and drive energy, and with exciton–magnon coupling preserved after patterning.
why: It connects magnetic dynamics directly to strong optical resonances, opening a route to low-energy optical modulation and coherent photonic processing.

title: Sample-resolved magnetic phase identification in RuO2
open: Is there a reproducible sample preparation route — a specific composition, strain state, defect population, or interface — in which RuO2 hosts altermagnetic order, or are the positive reports artifacts? A convincing answer would identify the sample-resolved conditions under which altermagnetic order appears, reconciling the affirmative claims with the direct null measurements.
status: RuO2 remains contested: 2024 μSR/neutron work (Keßler et al. (2024), "Absence of magnetic order in RuO2: insights from μSR spectroscopy and neutron diffraction," arXiv:2405.10820) and 2025 bulk quantum-oscillation work (Qian et al. (2025), "Determining the Nature of Magnetism in Altermagnetic Candidate RuO2," arXiv:2504.21138) support nonmagnetic interpretations. This does not negate established altermagnetism elsewhere.
solved_when: Either a reproducibly prepared RuO2 sample (with specified composition, strain state, defects, or interfaces) is shown by direct probes to host altermagnetic order, or the positive observations are traced to identifiable artifacts, yielding a consistent sample-resolved picture across measurement modalities.
why: It settles whether the RuO2 controversy is a sample-dependent materials issue or a symptom of a deeper problem, cleanly separating it from the validity of altermagnetism as a broader symmetry class.
key_works: Keßler et al. (2024), “Absence of magnetic order in RuO2: insights from μSR spectroscopy and neutron diffraction,” [arXiv:2405.10820](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.10820); Qian et al. title: Proton-driven magnetism with joint speed, retention, and endurance
open: Can a proton-driven magnetoelectric device switch rapidly, hold its magnetic state without power, and survive long cycling — all at once, under controlled humidity and temperature? Formally, the goal is to demonstrate rapid proton-gated switching together with nonvolatile retention and long cycling lifetime under such controlled conditions.
status: Solid-state proton pumps enabled reversible room-temperature anisotropy control in 2018–2019; however, faster proton transport can increase spontaneous state drift, creating tension between speed and retention. Key work: Tan et al. (2019), "Magneto-ionic control of magnetism using a solid-state proton pump," [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41563-018-0211-5).
solved_when: A device achieves rapid proton-gated switching, nonvolatile retention, and long cycling lifetime simultaneously, demonstrated under controlled humidity and temperature.
why: It would enable low-voltage magnetic reconfiguration, since protons rather than electrons or heavy ions do the gating.
key_works: Tan et al. (2019), “Magneto-ionic control of magnetism using a solid-state proton pump,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41563-018-0211-5).

title: Chemical suppression of vibronic quantum tunneling
open: Can a molecule's chemical environment — its vibrations and surroundings — be deliberately tuned to suppress zero-field quantum tunneling of magnetization, without inadvertently opening faster thermal relaxation channels? The goal is to identify such vibronic mechanisms and then demonstrate experimentally that chemically controlled tunneling rates agree with microscopic models.
status: A 2024 nonperturbative treatment shows vibration effects even without thermally occupied modes (Mattioni et al. (2024), "Vibronic effects on the quantum tunnelling of magnetisation in Kramers single-molecule magnets," [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-44486-3)). Reliable chemical design rules remain open.
solved_when: Specific vibrations and environments are identified that suppress zero-field tunneling, and chemical control of these is experimentally shown to yield tunneling rates consistent with microscopic models, without introducing faster thermal relaxation channels.
why: It removes relaxation pathways that high anisotropy barriers leave untouched, blocking a magnetic relaxation route that energy barriers alone cannot close.
key_works: Mattioni et al. (2024), “Vibronic effects on the quantum tunnelling of magnetisation in Kramers single-molecule magnets,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-44486-3).

title: Preserving molecular magnetic performance on surfaces
open: Can high-performance magnetic molecules be deposited onto surfaces with controlled orientation while still retaining their bulk relaxation behavior and hysteresis — that is, can we disentangle and separately control decomposition, ligand-field changes, and substrate effects during deposition and contacting?
status: Surface-supported hysteresis has been demonstrated, but a 2024 assessment by Gabarró-Riera and Sañudo (2024), "Challenges for exploiting nanomagnet properties on surfaces" ([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42004-024-01183-6)), identifies retention of the best properties during deposition and contacting as an unresolved problem.
solved_when: High-performance molecules are deposited with controlled orientation on a surface and shown to retain their bulk magnetic relaxation and hysteresis, with decomposition, ligand-field changes, and substrate effects experimentally separated.
why: It is the bridge between molecular synthesis and actual functional components; without it, the best molecular magnets cannot be turned into usable devices.
key_works: Gabarró-Riera and Sañudo (2024), “Challenges for exploiting nanomagnet properties on surfaces,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42004-024-01183-6).

title: Early fault detection throughout long HTS windings
open: Can a developing resistive region anywhere along a long high-temperature-superconducting (HTS) winding be detected early enough to act, despite noisy pickup signals, current redistribution within the cable, and the inaccessibility of cable interiors? The goal is a validated detection scheme with quantified missed-event and false-alarm rates.
status: Slow normal-zone propagation has complicated HTS magnet protection for decades. In 2022, termination-based current-redistribution monitoring was demonstrated in superconducting fusion cables by Teyber et al. (2022), “Current distribution monitoring enables quench and damage detection in superconducting fusion magnets,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-022-26592-2).
solved_when: A fault-detection method covers the full length of the winding and comes with experimentally validated missed-event and false-alarm rates, while remaining robust to pickup and current redistribution and applicable to regions that cannot be probed directly inside the cable.
why: It enables protection of costly superconducting magnets without resorting to excessive operating-current margins, which would otherwise degrade performance.
key_works: Teyber et al. (2022), “Current distribution monitoring enables quench and damage detection in superconducting fusion magnets,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-022-26592-2).

title: Repeatedly demountable high-current fusion joints
open: Can magnet joints be built that can be taken apart and reassembled many times while still carrying the enormous currents a fusion reactor demands — that is, can remotely separable, reusable joints retain low resistance, current uniformity, mechanical integrity, and acceptable cryogenic heat load under realistic contamination and alignment errors?

(2015), "ARC: A compact, high-field, fusion nuclear science facility and demonstration power plant with demountable magnets," [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fusengdes.2015.07.008)), and low-resistance joints have since advanced; qualification over a reactor lifecycle remains open.
solved_when: Such joints are qualified over a full reactor lifecycle under realistic contamination and alignment tolerances, preserving low resistance, current uniformity, structural integrity, and acceptable cryogenic heat load.
why: Demountable joints make it possible to replace internal reactor components without discarding the entire magnet system.
key_works: Sorbom et al. (2015), “ARC: A compact, high-field, fusion nuclear science facility and demonstration power plant with demountable magnets,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fusengdes.2015.07.008).

title: Accelerator-quality dipoles above 20 T
open: Can we build a full-length accelerator dipole that reliably reaches fields above 20 T while meeting every collider requirement — beam-quality field harmonics, useful aperture, safe quench energy extraction, and economical series production?

solved_when: Long, reproducible dipole magnets exceed 20 T while simultaneously delivering accelerator-quality harmonics, sufficient aperture, safe energy extraction, and manufacturability at series-production cost.
why: Such magnets raise the collision energy a collider can reach within a fixed tunnel, directly determining the reach of future accelerators.

why: It would combine ambient-temperature magnetic order with tunable semiconductor carriers, the prerequisite for diluted-magnetic-semiconductor devices that work outside the cryostat.

title: Practical broadband quantum advantage in magnetometry
open: Can a compact magnetometer that exploits squeezing or entanglement genuinely beat the best separable-probe protocol under fair, matched conditions? Formally, the advantage must hold at equal volume, photon flux, bandwidth, and total power, counting all costs of state preparation and readout.

why: A resource-fair advantage would justify smaller field instruments for science, navigation, and inspection; without it, claims of quantum advantage in magnetometry remain unproven in practice.

title: Practical four-state ferrotoroidic materials
open: Can a material be made in which all four ferrotoroidic domain states can be independently written, read, and retained at room temperature using practically accessible fields? In particular, can this four-state operation be preserved in thin films over repeated switching cycles?

title: Switchable polarity in metallic ferromagnets
open: Can the polar distortion of a ferromagnetic metal be switched back and forth with an electric field, in a way that is demonstrably not a charging effect, ion migration, heating, or current-induced torque? In other words, is genuine reversible structural-polarity control achievable in a metal that is also ferromagnetic?

(2024), “A correlated ferromagnetic polar metal by design,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41563-024-01856-6)), and current-driven magnetic switching followed in 2026 (Shi et al. (2026), “A Ferromagnetic Polar Metal With Efficient Electrical Switch of Magnetism,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/adma.74269)); neither result alone demonstrates reversal of the polar distortion.
solved_when: A ferromagnetic metal is shown to exhibit reversible electric-field-driven reversal of its polar distortion, with experiments that exclude charging, ion migration, heating, and current torques as the switching mechanism.
why: It would tie metallic transport to controllably switchable structural symmetry, opening polar-metal functionality to the conducting regime where ferroelectricity is normally screened away.

title: Rigorous Néel order in the square-lattice spin-1/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnet
open: Does the nearest-neighbor spin-1/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnet on the square lattice have Néel (antiferromagnetic) order in its ground state, in the sense of a rigorously proved nonzero staggered magnetization in the infinite-volume limit? In other words, prove that the ground state of this Hamiltonian exhibits long-range staggered order.
status: Decades of numerical evidence support ordering. Reflection-positivity arguments, as developed in work such as Dyson, Lieb, and Simon (1978), "Phase transitions in quantum spin systems with isotropic and nonisotropic interactions," [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01106729), establish related higher-spin and higher-dimensional cases (see also Tasaki (2020), *Physics and Mathematics of Quantum Many-Body Systems*, [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-41265-4)), but leave this central case open.
solved_when: A proof is given that the infinite-volume ground state of the nearest-neighbor square-lattice spin-1/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnet has nonzero staggered magnetization.
why: It would place the standard microscopic model of antiferromagnetism on rigorous footing, anchoring decades of physics intuition in mathematics.
key_works: Dyson, Lieb, and Simon (1978), “Phase transitions in quantum spin systems with isotropic and nonisotropic interactions,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01106729); Tasaki (2020), *Physics and Mathematics of Quantum Many-Body Systems*, [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-41265-4).

title: Nearest-neighbor kagome Heisenberg ground state
open: Is the spin-1/2 nearest-neighbor kagome Heisenberg antiferromagnet gapped or gapless in its ground state, and does that ground state carry topological order or break any symmetries? A definitive answer requires numerical extrapolations that are mutually consistent across methods.

(2026), "Comment on 'Spin-1/2 Kagome Heisenberg Antiferromagnet: Machine Learning Discovery of the Spinon Pair-Density-Wave Ground State,'" [arXiv:2605.28861](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.28861) challenges the sampling underlying a 2025 spinon pair-density-wave claim; unusually low variational energies alone do not settle the state. open: Can a ThMn12-type Sm–Fe magnet be made manufacturable in bulk while keeping the high magnetization and anisotropy of the intrinsic phase, achieving strong coercivity without diluting performance with excessive stabilizer elements?
status: An anisotropic sintered magnet reached approximately 1 T coercivity in 2021 (Zhang et al. (2021), "Origin of coercivity in an anisotropic Sm(Fe,Ti,V)12-based sintered magnet," [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actamat.2021.117161)); secondary phases and boundary control still separate bulk performance from intrinsic potential.
solved_when: A manufacturable bulk ThMn12-type Sm–Fe magnet retains high magnetization and anisotropy and achieves strong coercivity, with stabilizer content low enough that bulk performance matches the intrinsic potential.
why: It would deliver strong permanent magnets with substantially lower rare-earth content than today's materials.
key_works: Zhang et al. (2021), “Origin of coercivity in an anisotropic Sm(Fe,Ti,V)12-based sintered magnet,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actamat.2021.117161).

title: High-iron Sm–Co magnets with stable pinning networks
open: Can iron-rich Sm–Co permanent magnets be made whose magnetization gain from Fe substitution survives real service — retaining reproducible cellular pinning structure and coercivity over prolonged high-temperature use?
status: Sm2Co17-type magnets already serve hot applications, and atomic-scale studies connect chemistry, cellular structure, and domain wall pinning — notably Duerrschnabel et al. (2017), "Atomic structure and domain wall pinning in samarium-cobalt-based permanent magnets" ([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-017-00059-9)) — but higher Fe content and lifetime remain coupled, unresolved constraints.
solved_when: A higher-Fe Sm2Co17-type magnet demonstrates both increased magnetization and a cellular pinning network with coercivity that remains reproducible throughout prolonged high-temperature service.
why: It would deliver more compact permanent magnets for demanding thermal environments where conventional materials fall short.
key_works: Duerrschnabel et al. (2017), “Atomic structure and domain wall pinning in samarium-cobalt-based permanent magnets,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-017-00059-9).

title: Defect-controlled coercivity in τ-MnAl
open: Can the twin boundaries, antiphase boundaries, and decomposition products that currently undo the hard-magnetic properties of τ-MnAl be controlled during processing, so that dense, textured τ-MnAl retains its magnetization and coercivity in bulk form?
status: Hard magnetic τ-MnAl is established, but its narrow stability window and reversal-active defects limit bulk performance. A 2025 multiscale study, Bhandari et al. (2025), "Enhancing stability, magnetic anisotropy, and coercivity of manganese aluminum: Machine learning, ab initio, and micromagnetic modeling," [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevMaterials.9.034413), proposes substitutions that still require experimental validation.
solved_when: A processing route yields dense textured τ-MnAl in which the reversal-active defect populations (twins, antiphase boundaries, decomposition) are controlled sufficiently that the material retains its magnetization and coercivity after processing; computationally proposed substitutions must be experimentally validated.
why: Success would establish an inexpensive, rare-earth-free family of permanent magnets, reducing dependence on critical raw materials.
key_works: Bhandari et al. (2025), “Enhancing stability, magnetic anisotropy, and coercivity of manganese aluminum: Machine learning, ab initio, and micromagnetic modeling,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevMaterials.9.034413).

title: Alnico draw-annealing mechanism
open: Can we predict how draw annealing changes magnetization reversal in the interconnected Fe–Co nanorods of alnico, and use that understanding to design heat treatments that push the material toward its full coercivity potential?
status: Alnico has been industrially important since the 1930s. Microscopy and atom-probe studies show that chemical refinement alone does not explain the large draw-annealing coercivity increase — Zhou et al. (2018), "On spinodal decomposition in alnico—a transmission electron microscopy and atom probe tomography study" ([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actamat.2018.04.042)); see also Ke et al. (2017), "Simulation of alnico coercivity" ([arXiv:1707.04180](https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.04180)).
solved_when: A predictive model connects draw-annealing treatment parameters to the observed change in reversal behavior of the interconnected Fe–Co nanorods, and treatments designed from it approach alnico's coercivity potential.
why: It would improve an established rare-earth-free permanent magnet through controlled nanostructure rather than composition changes.
key_works: Zhou et al. (2018), “On spinodal decomposition in alnico—a transmission electron microscopy and atom probe tomography study,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actamat.2018.04.042); Ke et al. (2017), “Simulation of alnico coercivity,” [arXiv:1707.04180](https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.04180).

title: High-performance ferrites without La/Co additives
open: Can an M-type hexagonal ferrite magnet reach a substantially higher energy product using only abundant elements, by controlling texture, density, and grain boundaries, without relying on La or Co substitution?
status: Ferrites are mature commercial products; the open target is an improved cost–performance–criticality combination within their intrinsic magnetization limit. Key works: Pullar (2012), "Hexagonal ferrites: A review of the synthesis, properties and applications of hexaferrite ceramics," [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pmatsci.2012.04.001).
solved_when: A dense, well-textured, grain-boundary-engineered La-free, Co-free M-type ferrite demonstrates an improved cost–performance–criticality combination, approaching its intrinsic magnetization limit, relative to current commercial ferrites.
why: It upgrades the lowest-cost permanent-magnet platform, reducing dependence on critical elements while staying within ferrites' intrinsic magnetization limit.
key_works: Pullar (2012), “Hexagonal ferrites: A review of the synthesis, properties and applications of hexaferrite ceramics,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pmatsci.2012.04.001).

title: Three-dimensional printing of dense anisotropic magnets
open: Can we three-dimensionally print magnets with complex shapes and locally controlled orientation that approach the performance of dense, conventionally manufactured materials? Formally, the challenge is to achieve dense high-performance geometries while simultaneously controlling particle alignment, porosity, thermal damage, and dimensional error.
status: Large bonded Nd–Fe–B parts and anisotropic composites have been printed; however, binder dilution and process damage still constrain dense high-performance geometries. Key works include Li et al. (2016), “Big Area Additive Manufacturing of High Performance Bonded NdFeB Magnets,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/srep36212); and Gandha et al. (2018), “Additive manufacturing of anisotropic hybrid NdFeB-SmFeN nylon composite bonded magnets,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmmm.2018.07.021).
solved_when: Printed magnets with complex, locally oriented geometry are produced that approach dense conventional material performance, with alignment, porosity, thermal damage, and dimensional error all under control.
why: Success would enable magnetic circuits that are difficult or impossible to manufacture by conventional cutting and assembly.
key_works: Li et al. (2016), “Big Area Additive Manufacturing of High Performance Bonded NdFeB Magnets,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/srep36212); Gandha et al. (2018), “Additive manufacturing of anisotropic hybrid NdFeB-SmFeN nylon composite bonded magnets,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmmm.2018.07.021).

title: High-induction nanocrystalline cores at megahertz frequencies
open: Can a nanocrystalline soft magnetic core be engineered to combine near-2 T saturation induction with genuinely low loss under megahertz-frequency excitation, all while withstanding DC bias and elevated operating temperature and retaining economical processing?
status: FINEMM and Fe-rich alloy families currently supply different combinations of saturation induction and magnetic softness, with no single family delivering all desired properties at once. Eddy currents, anisotropy, resistivity, and manufacturing cost remain coupled constraints that cannot be optimized independently. Key works: Yoshizawa, Oguma, and Yamauchi (1988), “New Fe-based soft magnetic alloys composed of ultrafine grain structure,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.342149); Silveyra et al. (2018), “Soft magnetic materials for a sustainable and electrified world,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aao0195).
solved_when: A nanocrystalline core is demonstrated that simultaneously achieves near-2 T saturation induction and low loss under a declared megahertz-frequency excitation, specified DC bias, and specified operating temperature, while keeping the manufacturing route economically viable.
why: Such a core enables smaller inductors and transformers for fast power electronics.
key_works: Yoshizawa, Oguma, and Yamauchi (1988), “New Fe-based soft magnetic alloys composed of ultrafine grain structure,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.342149); Silveyra et al. (2018), “Soft magnetic materials for a sustainable and electrified world,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aao0195).

title: Economical rolling of high-silicon electrical steel
open: Can Fe–6.5 wt% Si sheet be produced thin, wide, and at high yield by an economical process, without losing the alloy's magnetic performance or its mechanical integrity? Formally, the goal is a rolling or equivalent route that avoids the ordered-phase embrittlement that blocks inexpensive conventional processing.
status: High-silicon sheet and alternative deposition or rapid-solidification routes exist, but ordered-phase embrittlement obstructs inexpensive conventional rolling. See Ouyang et al. (2019), "Review of Fe-6.5 wt%Si high silicon steel—A promising soft magnetic material for sub-kHz application," [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmmm.2019.02.089).
solved_when: Thin, wide Fe–6.5 wt% Si sheet is produced at high yield and competitive cost while retaining magnetic performance and mechanical integrity.
why: It would cut core losses in power conversion using a well-understood alloy system, avoiding the cost barriers of current specialty routes.
key_works: Ouyang et al. (2019), “Review of Fe-6.5 wt%Si high silicon steel—A promising soft magnetic material for sub-kHz application,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmmm.2019.02.089).

title: Softness–strength coexistence in high-induction alloys
open: Can we design Fe–Co or Fe-rich alloys that retain high saturation magnetization and low hysteresis loss even after being engineered for strength, fatigue resistance, and thermal stability, as needed in high-speed rotors?
status: Strengthening alters defects, stress states, or phases that also affect domain walls, so the magnetic and mechanical properties are currently optimized separately in different materials; no existing alloy addresses the full combination.
solved_when: An Fe–Co or Fe-rich alloy is demonstrated that combines high saturation and low hysteresis with the strength, fatigue resistance, and thermal stability required for high-speed rotor service.
why: It would permit faster, lighter electrical machines without sacrificing magnetic efficiency.
key_works: Silveyra et al. (2018), “Soft magnetic materials for a sustainable and electrified world,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aao0195); Coey (2010), *Magnetism and Magnetic Materials*.

title: Thermally stable insulation in soft magnetic composites
open: Can a soft magnetic composite be built whose insulating particle coatings survive both the compaction and the stress-relief annealing steps? Formally, the goal is a thin coating that withstands pressing and annealing without allowing electrical percolation between particles or excessively diluting the magnetic properties of the composite.
status: Phosphate, oxide, polymer, and hybrid coatings currently exist. Pushing toward stronger compaction and hotter annealing improves some material properties, but simultaneously damages the insulation or induces unwanted reactions at the particle interfaces. An overview is given by Périgo, Weidenfeller, Kollár, and Füzer (2018), "Past, present, and future of soft magnetic composites," [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.5027045).
solved_when: A thin coating design is demonstrated that endures compaction and stress-relief annealing while the compacted core remains electrically non-percolating and its magnetic properties are not excessively diluted by the coating.
why: It unlocks efficient three-dimensional magnetic cores with lower eddy-current loss, a key requirement for high-performance power conversion.
key_works: Périgo, Weidenfeller, Kollár, and Füzer (2018), “Past, present, and future of soft magnetic composites,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.5027045).

title: Long-term stability of nanocrystalline soft magnets
open: Can we predict — and then suppress — the slow degradation of nanocrystalline soft magnets over years of service, as grain growth, stress relaxation, and anisotropy drift accumulate under combined thermal cycling and mechanical loading?
status: Controlled nanocrystallization and stress annealing yield excellent initial properties, but short annealing tests do not establish service lifetime under coupled stresses. Foundational context: Herzer (2013), "Modern soft magnets: Amorphous and nanocrystalline materials," [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actamat.2012.10.040).
solved_when: A validated predictive model (or stabilization method) demonstrates control of grain growth, stress relaxation, and anisotropy drift over multi-year equivalent service under coupled thermal cycling and mechanical loading, with accelerated-aging tests established as valid proxies for that lifetime.
why: It would let compact, hot-running magnetic cores be trusted in long-lived equipment, where today's short annealing tests cannot establish service lifetime under coupled stresses.
key_works: Herzer (2013), “Modern soft magnets: Amorphous and nanocrystalline materials,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actamat.2012.10.040).

title: Hysteresis loss under arbitrary transient waveforms
open: Can we predict vector hysteresis behavior and core loss in soft magnetic materials under arbitrary transient waveforms — including minor loops, DC-bias changes, and temperature drift — with error bounds that transfer across materials and operating histories?
status: Classical loss models and learned models are useful in practice. MagNetX (Kwon et al. (2025), “MagNetX: Extending the MagNet Database for Modeling Power Magnetics in Transient,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1109/APEC48143.2025.10977252)) measured transients in 2025, building on foundations such as Bertotti (1988), “General properties of power losses in soft ferromagnetic materials,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1109/20.43994); a model generalizing across materials and operating histories remains open.
solved_when: A model exists that predicts vector hysteresis and loss during waveform transitions, minor loops, DC-bias changes, and temperature drift, with transferable error bounds that hold across materials and operating histories.
why: Without it, designers of real switching circuits risk inefficient or undersized magnetic cores; with it, core sizing and efficiency estimation under realistic transient operation become reliable.
key_works: Bertotti (1988), “General properties of power losses in soft ferromagnetic materials,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1109/20.43994); Kwon et al. (2025), “MagNetX: Extending the MagNet Database for Modeling Power Magnetics in Transient,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1109/APEC48143.2025.10977252).

title: Predicting cutting and assembly losses in motor laminations
open: Can the magnetic losses of an assembled motor core be predicted from the degradation introduced by manufacturing — cutting damage, burrs, joining, and clamping — together with the rotating flux conditions it actually experiences, rather than from measurements on pristine sheets? In other words, is there a model that maps process-induced damage to lamination losses under realistic rotating-flux excitation?
status: Local damage models and manufacturing measurements exist, but their spatial laws and parameters remain process-dependent, so no general prediction of assembled-core losses is yet available. Silveyra et al. (2018), “Soft magnetic materials for a sustainable and electrified world,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aao0195); Bertotti (1988), “General properties of power losses in soft ferromagnetic materials,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1109/20.43994).
solved_when: A predictive model quantitatively reproduces assembled motor-core losses from measured cutting damage, burrs, joining, and clamping effects under rotating flux, replacing reliance on pristine-sheet measurements, with spatial damage laws and parameters that are no longer process-dependent.
why: It closes the gap between material datasheets and actual machine efficiency, allowing motor designs to be evaluated with the losses the manufactured core will really exhibit.
key_works: Silveyra et al. (2018), “Soft magnetic materials for a sustainable and electrified world,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aao0195); Bertotti (1988), “General properties of power losses in soft ferromagnetic materials,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1109/20.43994).

title: Useful permeability under simultaneous DC bias and heat
open: Can soft magnetic cores be designed so that incremental permeability and losses remain predictable when DC bias, ripple frequency, and elevated temperature act together near saturation? A formal goal is a ferrite or powder core whose combined operating envelope is specified and reliable, not merely characterized at zero bias.
status: Distributed-gap composites and optimized ferrites address parts of the problem, but favorable zero-bias measurements do not establish performance over the combined bias–frequency–temperature envelope. Key works: Périgo et al. (2018), “Past, present, and future of soft magnetic composites,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.5027045); Li et al. (2023), “Why MagNet: Quantifying the Complexity of Modeling Power Magnetic Material Characteristics,” [publication](https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/why-magnet-quantifying-the-complexity-of-modeling-power-magnetic-/).
solved_when: A core design is demonstrated whose incremental permeability and loss under simultaneous DC bias, ripple frequency, and temperature near saturation are predictable within stated tolerances across that combined envelope, rather than extrapolated from zero-bias measurements.
why: It increases the usable energy storage in compact inductors, directly extending what power-conversion designs can extract from a given core.
key_works: Périgo et al. (2018), “Past, present, and future of soft magnetic composites,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.5027045); Li et al. (2023), “Why MagNet: Quantifying the Complexity of Modeling Power Magnetic Material Characteristics,” [publication](https://collaborate.princeton.edu/en/publications/why-magnet-quantifying-the-complexity-of-modeling-power-magnetic-/).

title: Sharp permeability–bandwidth bounds for structured magnets
open: For a heterogeneous, anisotropic, spatially dispersive magnetic composite operating under stated passivity assumptions, what is the true optimum trade-off among permeability, bandwidth, loss, and loading — and can that optimum be realized?
status: Snoek-type laws and their generalizations exist, but exceeding an isotropic formula by changing assumptions does not settle the optimum for a specified architecture. Key work: Acher and Dubourg (2008), "Generalization of Snoek's law to ferromagnetic films and composites," [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.77.104440). Related lines include Bode–Fano matching limits and passive-metamaterial bounds.
solved_when: Tight, realizable bounds on the permeability–bandwidth–loss–loading trade-off are derived for such composites under the stated passivity assumptions, showing they are sharp (attainable by an explicit architecture) rather than merely indicative.
why: It separates architecture changes that genuinely improve performance from specifications that are physically impossible, giving designers a certificate of optimality instead of heuristic guidance.
key_works: Acher and Dubourg (2008), “Generalization of Snoek’s law to ferromagnetic films and composites,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.77.104440).

title: Tenfold smaller magnetics at unchanged system loss
open: Reduce complete transformer or inductor volume tenfold against a declared baseline while preserving power, efficiency, isolation, temperature rise, lifetime, and electromagnetic compatibility.
status: Proposed system-level moonshot. Higher frequencies and new cores offer routes, but winding, insulation, cooling, and parasitic losses must be counted.
why: Shrinks chargers, converters, and power distribution hardware.
key_works: McHenry, Willard, and Laughlin (1999), “Amorphous and nanocrystalline materials for applications as soft magnets,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0079-6425(99)00002-X); Herzer (2013), “Modern soft magnets,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actamat.2012.10.040).

title: Granular FePt HAMR write–retention window under grain-size scaling
open: Can Curie-temperature dispersion in smaller L10-FePt grains be reduced while still preserving thermal retention and low write jitter, so that HAMR achieves higher recording density under declared heating and field budgets?

(2025), “Anisotropic Exchange Spin Model to Investigate the Curie Temperature Dispersion of Finite-Size L10-FePt Magnetic Nanoparticles,” [arXiv:2502.15247](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.15247), attributes approximately 70% of measured Curie-temperature dispersion to grain-size effects; the residual dispersion and joint write–retention performance remain open.

why: It extends disk areal density without sacrificing data stability — the core trade-off currently limiting HAMR scaling.

title: HAMR protection-stack lifetime at tighter head–disk spacing
open: Can a thinner overcoat–lubricant protection stack survive the repeated heating and intermittent contact of heat-assisted magnetic recording, and can its lifetime be predicted with confidence? The goal is stacks at reduced head–disk spacing whose decomposition, lubricant reflow, and debris generation under repeated HAMR thermal cycling are quantitatively validated.

(2024), "In-situ sub-angstrom characterization of laser-lubricant interaction in a thermo-tribological system," https://doi.org/10.1038/s44172-024-00284-3), and reactive simulations in 2025 identify shear-driven degradation (Shekhar et al. (2025), "ReaxFF molecular dynamics study of mechanochemical degradation of PFPE lubricants on DLC in heat-assisted magnetic recording," https://doi.org/10.1039/D5MR00023H). Durability at progressively thinner protection remains unresolved.
solved_when: Thinner overcoat–lubricant stacks are demonstrated to withstand repeated HAMR heating and intermittent contact, with validated lifetime predictions covering decomposition, reflow, and debris.
why: Without such stacks, interface degradation becomes the bottleneck on recording density, blocking gains from tighter head–disk spacing.
key_works: Cheng et al. (2024), “In-situ sub-angstrom characterization of laser-lubricant interaction in a thermo-tribological system,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s44172-024-00284-3); Shekhar et al. title: Sub-10-nanometre STT memory with simultaneous retention and writeability
open: Can spin-transfer-torque magnetic memory be scaled to sub-10-nanometre junction dimensions while still working reliably in arrays? In other words, can arrays of such junctions simultaneously meet declared retention, write-error, read-disturb, endurance, and yield requirements?

Joint array reliability and current delivery remain unresolved.
solved_when: A sub-10-nanometre spin-transfer-torque junction array is demonstrated that meets its declared retention, write-error, read-disturb, endurance, and yield requirements simultaneously.
why: It extends nonvolatile working memory to smaller dimensions.
key_works: Watanabe et al. (2018), “Shape anisotropy revisited in single-digit nanometer magnetic tunnel junctions,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-018-03003-7).

title: Predicting magnetic-memory write-error tails from microstructure
open: Can we predict the extremely rare failed or delayed write events in magnetic memory directly from measured microstructural defects, thermal fluctuations, and pulse waveforms? In particular, can the far-tail failure probabilities be validated without separately fitted effective temperatures?
status: Single-shot measurements have resolved the incubation and reversal stages of switching since 2020, as in Grimaldi et al. (2020), “Single-shot dynamics of spin–orbit torque and spin transfer torque switching in three-terminal magnetic tunnel junctions,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41565-019-0607-7). Extrapolating these observations to tiny failure probabilities under production variation remains open.
solved_when: A predictive framework reproduces the measured write-error tails — including rare failed and delayed writes — from measured defect data, thermal fluctuation statistics, and pulse waveforms, with tail validation achieved using no independently fitted effective-temperature parameters.
why: Device qualification hinges on failures that average switching curves completely hide; without tail prediction from microstructure, rare write errors under production variation cannot be certified.
key_works: Grimaldi et al. (2020), “Single-shot dynamics of spin–orbit torque and spin transfer torque switching in three-terminal magnetic tunnel junctions,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41565-019-0607-7).

title: Absolute spin-torque metrology across dissimilar interfaces
open: Can a single set of samples be measured by multiple traceable methods that separately determine the bulk spin generation, interfacial transmission, spin-memory loss, and torque absorption, rather than a correlated combination of these? Formally, the goal is an experimental decomposition of the total spin-to-torque conversion into its bulk and interfacial contributions with cross-method agreement on identical specimens.
status: Interfacial spin-memory loss was quantified by Rojas-Sánchez et al. (2014), “Spin Pumping and Inverse Spin Hall Effect in Platinum: The Essential Role of Spin-Memory Loss at Metallic Interfaces,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.112.106602). Bulk and interface parameters remain correlated in material-dependent inverse problems.
solved_when: Traceable, independent measurements on the same samples yield separately resolved values for bulk spin generation, interfacial transmission, spin-memory loss, and torque absorption that agree across methods within stated uncertainties, breaking the correlation in the material-dependent inverse problem.
why: Without such a decomposition, comparisons of candidate torque sources conflate bulk and interface effects, making rankings of materials unreliable; with it, torque-source comparisons become meaningful.
key_works: Rojas-Sánchez et al. (2014), “Spin Pumping and Inverse Spin Hall Effect in Platinum: The Essential Role of Spin-Memory Loss at Metallic Interfaces,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.112.106602).

title: Quantitative orbital-to-spin conversion in light-metal torque devices
open: Can the orbital angular momentum carried by light metals be converted into magnetic torque efficiently enough — and reproducibly enough — to switch a magnet? Specifically, how large is the orbital contribution to the torque, where in the heterostructure does the orbital-to-spin conversion occur, and how does it depend on disorder and interface chemistry?
status: Long-range orbital transport and large orbital torque were reported in 2023 by Hayashi et al. (2023), "Observation of long-range orbital transport and giant orbital torque," [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42005-023-01139-7). Whether the reported efficiencies transfer across devices and survive realistic manufacturing conditions remains unresolved.
solved_when: A quantitative accounting of the orbital contribution to torque, its conversion location, and its dependence on disorder and interface chemistry is established, together with a demonstration of complete magnetization switching at lower energy than matched control devices.
why: It extends efficient torque generation beyond scarce, heavy elements, opening a cheaper and lighter materials palette for spintronic memory and logic.
key_works: Hayashi et al. (2023), “Observation of long-range orbital transport and giant orbital torque,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42005-023-01139-7).

title: Topological-insulator torque after full device processing
open: Can a topological insulator retain its useful spin–charge conversion after surviving the full manufacturing sequence — deposition, patterning, contacting, and thermal processing — in an integrated memory cell? Success would be demonstrated by reduced complete write energy in such a processed cell.
status: Sputtered bismuth–selenium films showed large room-temperature torque in 2018, as reported by Mahendra DC et al. (2018), “Room-temperature high spin–orbit torque due to quantum confinement in sputtered BiₓSe₍₁−ₓ₎ films” (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41563-018-0136-z). Surface contributions, bulk conduction, shunting, and process compatibility remain coupled problems.
solved_when: A topological-insulator device that has undergone deposition, patterning, contacting, and thermal processing still shows useful spin–charge conversion, and an integrated cell exhibits reduced complete write energy compared to the relevant baseline.
why: It tests whether topological states offer a practical memory advantage rather than a laboratory-only effect; without process compatibility the torque observed in pristine films cannot translate into usable low-energy writing.
key_works: Mahendra DC et al. (2018), “Room-temperature high spin–orbit torque due to quantum confinement in sputtered BiₓSe₍₁−ₓ₎ films,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41563-018-0136-z).

title: Timing-tolerant voltage-controlled magnetic switching
open: Can a voltage-controlled magnetic element be switched deterministically in both directions across broad ranges of pulse width and temperature, while preserving nonvolatile retention and low leakage? Formally, the goal is a construction whose switching outcome is insensitive to pulse timing and thermal dispersion over wide operating windows.
status: Coherent voltage-pulse switching was demonstrated in 2012 by Shiota et al. (2012), “Induction of coherent magnetization switching in a few atomic layers of FeCo using voltage pulses,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/nmat3172). Timing sensitivity, thermal dispersion, and retention–anisotropy tradeoffs remain coupled obstacles.
solved_when: A demonstrated switching scheme achieves deterministic bidirectional voltage-controlled-anisotropy switching over broad pulse-width and temperature windows while retaining nonvolatility and low leakage.
why: It would cut the energy of magnetic writing and shrink the required transistor area; without timing tolerance, voltage-controlled switching remains too fragile for practical memory use.

(2025), "Octupole-driven spin-transfer torque switching of all-antiferromagnetic tunnel junctions," [arXiv:2509.03026v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.03026v1). why: It would unite fast antiferromagnetic dynamics with convenient electrical readout, enabling a nonvolatile memory free of ferromagnetic stray-field limitations.

title: Complete picosecond Mn3Sn memory cycles
open: Can an antiferromagnetic Mn3Sn memory be driven through complete, sustained random-access cycles at picosecond speed — writing, selecting, reading, and thermally recovering — rather than demonstrating switching pulses alone?
