solved_when: A Mn3Sn device demonstrates sustained repeated memory cycles at timescales comparable to the reported 40-ps switching pulses, with all cycle components — selection, readout, thermal recovery, and interconnect delivery — integrated, and with measured errors and total energy reported.
why: It determines whether the antiferromagnetic speed advantage survives the overhead of a full circuit, deciding whether such devices can become a genuine memory technology or remain a laboratory curiosity.
key_works: Tsai et al. (2026), “Picosecond ultralow-power switching device based on an antiferromagnet,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adt3136).

title: Programmable synchronization of large spin-oscillator networks
open: Can a large network of spin-torque or spin Hall nano-oscillators be engineered so that its pairwise couplings and individual oscillator frequencies are independently programmable, and can the collective phase be kept locked despite device mismatch and noise — with quantitative scaling laws predicting when locking holds and when it fails?

why: It underpins practical microwave sources, associative memory, and analog optimization built from spin-oscillator arrays; without programmability and predictable locking, such devices cannot scale reliably.

(2026), “Integrated magnonic chip using cascaded logic,” [arXiv:2601.02644](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.02644).

title: Foundry-compatible low-damping patterned garnet films

open: Can magnonic circuits be equipped with programmable, cascadable nonreciprocal elements — isolators and circulators — that keep strong directional contrast over a useful bandwidth and power range while adding minimal insertion loss and requiring little bias overhead?

why: Such elements control reflections and back-action in dense wave circuits, which currently limit scalable magnonic network design.

title: Universality of phase ordering in finite-lifetime magnon condensates
open: Do magnon condensates driven far from equilibrium but living only a finite time still order their phase according to universal scaling laws? Determine the scaling behavior of spontaneous phase ordering, coherence growth, vortex formation, and defect annihilation in such condensates.
status: Room-temperature magnon condensation was reported in 2006, and spontaneous phase coherence was directly resolved in 2026 [Koster et al. (2026), "Emergence of phase coherence in a magnon Bose–Einstein condensate," DOI: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41567-026-03373-6]. The dynamical and universality questions remain open, with related directions including KPZ universality in driven condensates and nonequilibrium Kibble–Zurek scaling.
solved_when: Scaling laws for phase ordering, coherence growth, vortex dynamics, and defect annihilation are determined and shown to be universal (or demonstrably non-universal) for driven magnon condensates of finite lifetime.
why: It provides a direct experimental testbed for the statistical mechanics of open quantum fluids, where finite lifetime and drive prevent equilibrium assumptions from applying.
key_works: Koster et al. (2026), “Emergence of phase coherence in a magnon Bose–Einstein condensate,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41567-026-03373-6).

open: Can a nonclassical magnon state — a single magnon or an entangled magnon mode — be transferred, stored, and retrieved between independently addressable nodes with its measured coherence or entanglement preserved?

(2020), "Entanglement-based single-shot detection of a single magnon with a superconducting qubit," [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aaz9236). (2025), "Magnetic Materials for Quantum Magnonics," [arXiv:2510.09331](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.09331).

why: It would add magnetic memories and transducers to modular quantum systems, extending quantum networking beyond photon- and phonon-based buses.

title: Quantum-efficient magnon microwave–optical conversion
open: Can a single magnonic device convert quantum states bidirectionally between microwave and optical frequencies while preserving their nonclassical character — that is, achieving conversion efficiency, added noise, and bandwidth together sufficient for quantum-coherent transfer, with optical heating suppressed in the same device?
status: Bidirectional microwave–optical conversion was demonstrated in 2016 by Hisatomi et al. (2016), “Bidirectional conversion between microwave and light via ferromagnetic magnons,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.93.174427); a 2026 CrSBr preprint, Adak et al. (2026), “Microwave-to-optical transduction using magnon-exciton coupling in a layered antiferromagnet,” [arXiv:2604.03441](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.03441), reports broadband magnon–exciton transduction. solved_when: Bidirectional microwave–optical conversion is demonstrated with efficiency, added noise, and bandwidth sufficient to preserve nonclassical states, in a device where optical heating is suppressed.
why: Such a transducer would connect microwave-based quantum processors to optical networks, enabling long-distance quantum communication between them.
key_works: Hisatomi et al. (2016), “Bidirectional conversion between microwave and light via ferromagnetic magnons,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.93.174427); Adak et al. title: Useful topological magnon edge channels with damping and interactions
open: Can a topological magnon edge channel survive contact with reality — disorder, finite temperature, nonlinear scattering, and realistic damping — and still beat ordinary channels in a measurable transport metric? In other words, does band topology yield a practical edge-transport advantage for magnons, and can the boundaries where that advantage fails be mapped out?
status: Topological magnon bands are established research territory (McClarty (2022), "Topological Magnons: A Review," [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-conmatphys-031620-104715)), but no demonstration yet shows a usable edge-transport advantage under realistic conditions.
solved_when: An experiment demonstrates a topological magnon edge channel that retains a measurable transport advantage under disorder, temperature, nonlinear scattering, and realistic damping, and identifies the conditions at which the advantage is lost.
why: It directly tests whether topology improves practical magnonic wave transport; band topology alone does not guarantee long-lived, electrically usable edge information transport, so without this the field's central promise remains unverified.
key_works: McClarty (2022), “Topological Magnons: A Review,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-conmatphys-031620-104715).

title: Local tomography of nonequilibrium magnon distributions
open: Can the full frequency-, position-, and time-dependent occupation of a nonequilibrium magnon gas be measured locally, going beyond descriptions in terms of a single effective temperature or chemical potential, and can the measurement back-action be calibrated against independently measured currents?
status: NV magnetometry measured a local spin chemical potential in a magnetic insulator in 2017 (Du et al. (2017), "Control and local measurement of the spin chemical potential in a magnetic insulator," [arXiv:1611.07408](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.07408)), but strongly nonthermal magnon distributions remain incompletely observable.
solved_when: A reconstruction of magnon occupations resolved in frequency, position, and time is demonstrated for strongly nonthermal distributions, with the measurement back-action quantitatively calibrated against independent current measurements.
why: It supplies the missing distribution-function inputs that quantitative magnon transport and heating models currently lack.

title: Net refrigeration from the spin Peltier effect
open: Can the spin Peltier effect be made to cool a real load — that is, to remove a calibrated useful heat load once Joule heating, thermal shunts, and drive electronics are all accounted for — and thereby establish a genuine coefficient of performance?

solved_when: A device is demonstrated that removes a calibrated useful heat load, with the measured coefficient of performance reflecting losses from Joule heating, thermal shunts, and drive electronics.
why: It tests whether spin-mediated heat control can become practical cooling rather than a laboratory curiosity.

why: It would make reported conversion coefficients and screening results genuinely comparable between laboratories, rather than apparatus-dependent.

title: Complete femtosecond angular-momentum accounting
open: Can we account, channel by channel and with mutually compatible absolute calibrations, for where the angular momentum goes during femtosecond laser-induced demagnetization? That is, can spin angular momentum, electronic orbital motion, lattice motion, and angular momentum transported away from the sample all be measured time-resolved so that their sum closes the budget on sub-100-fs timescales?
status: Ultrafast demagnetization was observed in 1996, and direct evidence for lattice transfer of angular momentum appeared in 2019 (Dornes et al. (2019), “The ultrafast Einstein–de Haas effect,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-018-0822-7)). A complete sub-100-fs multichannel budget remains missing.
solved_when: A complete sub-100-fs multichannel angular-momentum budget is demonstrated, with spin, electronic orbital, lattice, and transport channels measured with compatible absolute calibrations that together close the time-resolved accounting during demagnetization.
why: A closed budget identifies the physical speed and dissipation limits of ultrafast magnetic switching, telling us which angular-momentum channels ultimately cap how fast magnetism can be controlled.
key_works: Dornes et al. (2019), “The ultrafast Einstein–de Haas effect,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-018-0822-7).

title: Predictive materials rule for single-pulse all-optical reversal
open: Is there a predictive rule that tells us, from a material's basic parameters alone, when a single femtosecond-scale laser pulse will deterministically reverse its magnetization? More formally, can a transferable criterion be derived that predicts deterministic switching windows from exchange, damping, sublattice moments, absorption, and heat flow?
status: Transient ferromagnetic-like alignment during reversal was measured in 2011 by Radu et al. (2011), "Transient ferromagnetic-like state mediating ultrafast reversal of antiferromagnetically coupled spins," [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature09901). Existing mechanisms do not yet constitute a general quantitative discovery rule.
solved_when: A quantitative, transferable criterion is derived that takes exchange, damping, sublattice moments, absorption, and heat flow as inputs and predicts deterministic single-pulse all-optical switching windows, validated as a general discovery rule rather than a case-by-case mechanism.
why: It would replace empirical composition searches with rational guidance, broadening the palette of candidate materials for fast optical memory.
key_works: Radu et al. (2011), “Transient ferromagnetic-like state mediating ultrafast reversal of antiferromagnetically coupled spins,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature09901).

title: Dense direct-overwrite optical magnetic arrays
open: Can an array of nanoscale magnetic cells be written by light so that any chosen cell is set directly to a desired state, without first reading it and without disturbing its neighbors optically or thermally? (2019), “Integrating all-optical switching with spintronics,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-018-08062-4). solved_when: Direct overwrite of either magnetic state into selected nanoscale cells of a dense array is demonstrated, repeatably and without neighboring optical and thermal disturbance, with the array's error distribution measured.
why: It would bridge femtosecond optical control of magnetization to practical random-access storage, turning laboratory switching demonstrations into a viable memory technology.

title: Microscopic origin and universality of magnetic inertia

open: Can one reliably write or erase a single magnetic skyrmion at a chosen site? The goal is an experimental or engineering scheme that creates or deletes exactly one skyrmion at a selected position with measured low failure probability, minimal disturbance of neighboring skyrmions, and reproducible energy over repeated write–erase cycles.

(2026), “The 2026 Skyrmionics Roadmap,” [arXiv:2601.16575](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.16575).

title: Predictive skyrmion lifetimes in disordered devices
subfield: Magnetic textures and artificial spin systems
open: Can we predict, from first principles, how long a skyrmion survives in a patterned magnetic film whose defects, edges, and nonuniform interactions shape its escape routes — without fitting an arbitrary attempt frequency? Formally, this asks for absolute lifetimes and escape pathways computed directly from a specified disorder landscape.
status: Atomistic calculations established skyrmion collapse and boundary escape in 2018 (Bessarab et al. (2018), "Lifetime of racetrack skyrmions," [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-018-21623-3)); mapping measured disorder to device lifetime distributions remains open.

title: Reconciliation of monolayer VSe2 magnetism

Sample-dependent outcomes remain incompletely reconciled.
solved_when: A reproducible phase map exists that accounts for magnetic signals as a function of substrate, stoichiometry, defects, strain, and charge-density-wave order, and cleanly separates intrinsic from reconstructed phases.
why: It would resolve a prominent materials-identification controversy, determining whether monolayer VSe2 is a genuine two-dimensional ferromagnet or whether reported signals arise from extrinsic or reconstructed conditions.

title: Reliable all-electrical altermagnetic memory
open: Can a practical memory cell be built entirely from an altermagnet, in which the compensated spin-split order can be switched electrically and read back reliably? Concretely, this means integrating independently verified order reversal with robust readout, low error rates, retention, and endurance, while establishing tolerance to domain and orientation variation.

(2026), "Altermagnetic spintronics," https://doi.org/10.1038/s41567-026-03337-w). A qualified nanoscale memory remains the target.

why: It would establish whether fast compensated spin-split materials can serve as useful electronics rather than laboratory curiosities, opening a route to memory devices without ferromagnets and their stray fields.

title: Absolute nonrelativistic spin-splitter efficiency
open: Can an altermagnetic spin splitter actually convert charge current into spin current with useful efficiency, rather than merely exhibiting spin-split bands? Concretely, this requires measuring the magnitude and angular structure of the altermagnetic spin current while cleanly separating spin–orbit, thermal, interfacial, and parasitic magnetic contributions.
status: Efficient nonrelativistic spin splitting was proposed in 2021 by González-Hernandez et al. (2021), "Efficient Electrical Spin Splitter Based on Nonrelativistic Collinear Antiferromagnetism," [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.126.127701), and band splitting has since been observed. However, band structure alone does not establish usable conversion efficiency.
solved_when: An absolute measurement of the altermagnetic spin-current magnitude and its angular structure is achieved, with spin–orbit, thermal, interfacial, and parasitic magnetic contributions experimentally disentangled.
why: It would test whether altermagnetism provides a distinct, potentially efficient spin-source mechanism, and determine whether band splitting alone translates into usable conversion efficiency.
key_works: González-Hernández et al. (2021), “Efficient Electrical Spin Splitter Based on Nonrelativistic Collinear Antiferromagnetism,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.126.127701).

why: It would enable compact magnetic memory elements written electrically, replacing current-driven switching with low-power electric-field control.

title: Magneto-ionic cycling without irreversible redox damage

solved_when: A device architecture with identified oxygen reservoirs and diffusion pathways demonstrates extended cycling that restores the same magnetic microstructure, verified by tracking chemistry and morphology (not just average magnetization) and showing no cumulative redox damage.
why: It establishes defensible lifetimes for electrically reconfigurable magnets; without it, apparent magnetic reversibility may mask cumulative damage that limits practical use.

title: Large reversible caloric changes without transition hysteresis

Compatibility engineering and alloying reduce losses, but large first-sweep responses need not maximize refrigeration. Gutfleisch et al. (2016), "Mastering hysteresis in magnetocaloric materials," [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1098/rsta.2015.0308).
solved_when: A material exhibits large reversible entropy and temperature changes under repeated low-field operation, with hysteresis reduced sufficiently that the reversible cycle — not merely the first sweep — delivers maximal refrigeration performance.
why: It determines the cooling efficiency and the magnetic field requirements of practical magnetocaloric refrigeration.

why: Without it, magnetocaloric cooling devices lose cooling capacity over time and risk coolant contamination from fractured particulate material.

title: Corrosion protection that survives magnetic breathing

solved_when: A protection scheme is demonstrated that maintains corrosion protection of a regenerator across its full lifetime — including coating defects, coolant changes, and magnetovolume cycling — while leaving flow channels unobstructed and heat exchange efficiency intact, and that remains robust across realistic production variation.
why: It makes efficient aqueous heat exchange compatible with reactive magnetocaloric refrigerants, a prerequisite for practical magnetic cooling devices.

open: Can refrigerants made only of abundant elements deliver hydrogen-liquefaction cooling across the 20–77 K window at performance levels matching rare-earth benchmarks under identical cyclic conditions, while surviving shaping and environmental exposure? (2024), "A matter of performance & criticality: a review of rare-earth-based magnetocaloric intermetallic compounds for hydrogen liquefaction," [arXiv:2405.01128](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.01128)). solved_when: An abundant-element refrigerant (or sequence of them) covering approximately 20–77 K demonstrates performance equal to rare-earth benchmarks under identical cyclic conditions, with properties retained after shaping and after environmental (e.g., moisture) exposure.
why: Replacing rare-earth refrigerants would cut material cost and ease supply constraints, making magnetic hydrogen liquefaction economically viable at scale.

title: Net advantage of combined magnetic and mechanical caloric cycles
open: When does driving a caloric material with both magnetic field and mechanical stress yield a genuine net gain in cooling performance, once the full energy ledger — actuator work, friction, thermal leakage, and fatigue — is accounted for? solved_when: A combined magnetic-and-mechanical caloric cycle is demonstrated that operates repeatably and whose total losses — including actuator work, friction, leakage, and fatigue — are shown to be reduced relative to the relevant baseline, with a complete energy accounting of the cycle.
why: It tests whether multicaloric control overcomes practical transition losses; material-level reversibility alone does not establish a superior refrigerator, so the engineering question of net advantage is what ultimately matters for these cooling cycles.

open: Can we predict the absolute spin-relaxation time of a molecular crystal purely from first principles, before any measurement of its relaxation rate? title: Individually addressable dense molecular-magnet arrays
open: Can a dense array of single-molecule magnets be written and read individually, with each molecule separately addressable and identifiable, without electrical contacts or inter-molecule dipolar interactions destroying independent bistability?
status: Single-molecule measurements and surface organization supply the necessary components, but scalable addressing, wiring, and minimally disturbing readout remain unresolved (Gabarró-Riera and Sañudo, 2024, “Challenges for exploiting nanomagnet properties on surfaces,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42004-024-01183-6)).
solved_when: A many-molecule array is demonstrated in which identified individual molecules can be written and read, with quantified crosstalk, error rates, retention, and fabrication yield.
why: It tests whether molecular-scale magnets deliver practically usable storage density rather than merely interesting physics.
key_works: Gabarró-Riera and Sañudo (2024), “Challenges for exploiting nanomagnet properties on surfaces,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42004-024-01183-6).

title: Reproducible microscopic origin of metal-free organic ferromagnetism
open: Can we explain, predictively, why some metal-free organic radicals order ferromagnetically at room temperature — identifying how radical structure, molecular packing, and exchange coupling combine to produce bulk order, with quantitative impurity accounting and independent replication to rule out spurious signals?
status: Room-temperature organic ferromagnetism has been reported. A 2025 study adds dichroism and microwave evidence in perylene-bisimide radicals — Yang et al. (2025), "Evidence of X-Ray Magnetic Circular Dichroism and Low-Field Microwave Absorption in Room-Temperature Organic Ferromagnetic Semiconductor," [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/idm2.70002) — but transferable synthesis rules remain open.
solved_when: A reproducible microscopic mechanism is established linking radical chemistry, packing, and exchange to bulk room-temperature ferromagnetic order, verified through quantitative impurity accounting, element-sensitive probes, and independent replication, together with transferable synthesis rules.
why: It would establish trustworthy foundations for lightweight, metal-free organic magnets; without it, reports of organic ferromagnetism remain unreliable as a basis for designing magnetic organic materials.
key_works: Yang et al. (2025), “Evidence of X-Ray Magnetic Circular Dichroism and Low-Field Microwave Absorption in Room-Temperature Organic Ferromagnetic Semiconductor,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/idm2.70002).

title: High-ordering-temperature molecular frameworks with useful magnetic strength
open: Can a molecular magnetic framework be engineered that combines a high ordering temperature with genuinely useful magnetic strength — that is, magnetization and energy density large enough for bulk applications — without sacrificing coercivity, processing stability, or controlled redox stoichiometry?
status: Chromium–pyrazine networks reached ordering temperatures up to 242 °C in 2020 (Perlepe et al. (2020), "Metal-organic magnets with large coercivity and ordering temperatures up to 242°C," [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.abb3861)), but strength, durability, and processing remain distinct, unresolved constraints.
solved_when: A molecular framework is demonstrated that retains an ordering temperature at least on the order of the current benchmark (ordering temperatures up to 242 °C) while achieving materially higher magnetization and usable energy density together with adequate coercivity, durability in processing, and controlled redox stoichiometry.
why: It would push molecular magnets from laboratory curiosities into functional bulk devices, for example in lightweight actuation, where molecular frameworks' tunability and low density become real advantages.
key_works: Perlepe et al. (2020), “Metal-organic magnets with large coercivity and ordering temperatures up to 242°C,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.abb3861).

title: Fatigue-resistant optical switching of molecular magnetic bistability
open: Can an organized molecular magnetic bistable system be switched optically, reversibly, over many cycles, without accumulating photochemical damage? A satisfactory answer would also quantify the retained states and the absorbed energy per operation.
status: A 2025 two-dimensional metal–organic framework demonstrated magnetic coercivity photomodulation (Wang et al. (2025), "Two-Dimensional Metal–Organic Framework with High-Performance Single-Molecule Magnets as Nodes Showing Magnetic Coercivity Photomodulation," https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.5c03704). Complete write–retain–erase operation and dense addressing remain open.
solved_when: A molecular magnetic bistable system demonstrates complete write–retain–erase optical operation over many switching cycles without photochemical fatigue, with the retained states and absorbed energy per operation established.
why: It would enable contact-free, optical reconfiguration of molecular magnets, a prerequisite for optical molecular memory.
key_works: Wang et al. (2025), “Two-Dimensional Metal–Organic Framework with High-Performance Single-Molecule Magnets as Nodes Showing Magnetic Coercivity Photomodulation,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.5c03704).

title: Damage-free protection of large-energy REBCO magnets
open: Can a full-scale, large-energy REBCO magnet be protected so that credible supply, joint, cooling, and local-conductor faults never produce excessive temperature, voltage, or stress, with coupled simulation models validated against experiments?
status: SPARC's model-coil program demonstrated approximately 20 T at large scale and conducted deliberate quench tests (Hartwig et al. (2024), "The SPARC Toroidal Field Model Coil Program," [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1109/TASC.2023.3332613)). Nonuniform dissipation and coupled failures remain central protection problems; screening currents have been shown to increase thermal quench propagation speed in ultra-high-field REBCO magnets (Pardo et al. (2025), [arXiv:2509.06621](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.06621)).
solved_when: A full-scale magnet withstands credible supply, joint, cooling, and local-conductor failure scenarios without exceeding temperature, voltage, or stress limits, and the coupled models used to predict this behavior are experimentally validated.
why: It makes compact fusion devices and other large HTS installations reliable and maintainable, since unprotected coupled failures can destroy expensive, hard-to-replace magnets.
key_works: Hartwig et al. (2024), “The SPARC Toroidal Field Model Coil Program,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1109/TASC.2023.3332613); Pardo et al. (2025), “Screening currents increase thermal quench propagation speed in ultra-high-field REBCO magnets,” [arXiv:2509.06621](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.06621).

title: Preventing REBCO delamination under combined cyclic loads
open: Can REBCO tape conductors be engineered so that they never delaminate irreversibly when transverse stress, bending, Lorentz forces, and thermal cycling act simultaneously — and can we predict production-length lifetimes with statistical confidence? Formally, the goal is a conductor-and-verification strategy that survives combined cyclic loads with defensible weakest-link lifetime statistics over full production lengths.
status: A longstanding constraint in high-field magnet engineering. A 2025 nested-coil study observed REBCO delamination following transitions below design current: Lu et al. (2025), "Observation of REBCO delamination in the resistive insulation nested coils," [arXiv:2512.16647](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.16647).
solved_when: A design and qualification procedure exists under which REBCO tape withstands simultaneous transverse stress, bending, Lorentz force, and thermal cycling without irreversible delamination, with lifetime predictions for production-length conductors supported by statistically defensible reliability evidence.
why: It converts the tape's intrinsic critical current into a dependable operating field; without it, magnets must be de-rated below design current to avoid delamination-driven failure.
key_works: Lu et al. (2025), “Observation of REBCO delamination in the resistive insulation nested coils,” [arXiv:2512.16647](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.16647).

title: Reactor-lifetime REBCO under fusion neutron exposure
open: Can we predict how the critical current and mechanical integrity of REBCO coated conductors evolve over a full reactor lifetime of fusion-neutron fluence, under the simultaneous operating conditions of cryogenic temperature, high magnetic field, mechanical stress, and periodic maintenance anneals?
status: In-situ cryogenic irradiation with fusion-spectrum neutrons was reported in 2026 by Adams et al. (2026), "The performance of REBCO coated conductor during in situ cryogenic irradiation with fusion-spectrum neutrons" ([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1088/1361-6668/ae4548)), establishing a combined-exposure dataset; lifetime extrapolation from such data remains the stronger, unsolved target.
solved_when: A validated predictive capability exists for critical current and mechanical integrity extrapolated to reactor-lifetime fusion-neutron fluence under combined temperature, field, stress, and annealing exposures, consistent with the reported in-situ cryogenic fusion-spectrum irradiation data.
why: Such a prediction directly determines magnet shielding requirements, conductor replacement schedules, and the achievable fusion power density of a plant.
key_works: Adams et al. (2026), “The performance of REBCO coated conductor during in situ cryogenic irradiation with fusion-spectrum neutrons,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1088/1361-6668/ae4548).

title: Tenfold cheaper qualified REBCO conductor
open: Can the delivered cost per unit of usable current–length of qualified REBCO conductor be reduced tenfold at specified field, temperature, stress, and yield? The target encompasses the full delivered price — including stabilization, inspection, rejects, and lifetime — rather than the bare strand cost.
status: Long conductors and large magnets already exist, but manufacturing cost and application-specific qualification still constrain deployment (Coombs et al. (2024), "High-temperature superconductors and their large-scale applications," [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s44287-024-00112-y)).
solved_when: A qualified REBCO conductor achieves a tenfold reduction in delivered cost per usable current–length at the specified field, temperature, stress, and yield conditions, with stabilization, inspection, reject rates, and lifetime included in the accounting.
why: It would broaden access to superconducting magnets for fusion, industrial, and research applications that are currently priced out.
key_works: Coombs et al. (2024), “High-temperature superconductors and their large-scale applications,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s44287-024-00112-y).

title: Reliable 40 T-class all-superconducting user magnets
open: Can an all-superconducting magnet reach approximately 40 tesla in a useful bore while remaining a dependable user facility instrument? Formally, this means sustaining a stable ~40 T field under manageable stress, cycling safely and repeatedly, and demonstrating the availability a user program requires.
status: The 2019 record of 45.5 T was achieved by combining an HTS insert with a resistive background field (Hahn et al. (2019), "45.5-tesla direct-current magnetic field generated with a high-temperature superconducting magnet," [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-019-1293-1)). All-superconducting systems have since advanced into the 30 T range, but reaching 40 T remains hindered by insulation and mechanical challenges, including REBCO delamination observed in resistive-insulation nested coils (Lu et al. (2025), [arXiv:2512.16647](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.16647)).
solved_when: An all-superconducting magnet delivers approximately 40 T with a useful bore, stable field, manageable stress, safe repeated cycling, and demonstrated facility availability.
why: It would provide sustained access to extreme magnetic fields at far lower electrical demand than resistive or hybrid systems, enabling continuous high-field experiments that today's power-hungry magnets cannot economically support.
key_works: Hahn et al. (2019), “45.5-tesla direct-current magnetic field generated with a high-temperature superconducting magnet,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-019-1293-1); Lu et al. (2025), “Observation of REBCO delamination in the resistive insulation nested coils,” [arXiv:2512.16647](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.16647).

title: Predictable screening-current field errors in HTS magnets
open: Can the field errors and long-term drift caused by screening currents in high-temperature superconducting magnets be predicted, and suppressed, across ramp profiles, thermal histories, and mechanical deformation — all without sacrificing current density or quench protection?
status: Simulations, conditioning procedures, and conductor modifications currently provide only partial control of screening-current effects; the coupling between field quality, forces, and hysteretic history remains significant, as reviewed in Zhou et al. (2023), "Review of progress and challenges of key mechanical issues in high-field superconducting magnets," [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1093/nsr/nwad001).
solved_when: A predictive framework is demonstrated that captures spatial field errors and drift from screening currents over realistic ramps, thermal cycling, and deformation, and achieves suppression of these errors while preserving current density and magnet protection margins.
why: It would enable stable, drift-free fields for NMR spectroscopy, imaging, and accelerator magnets, where screening-current-induced errors currently degrade field quality.
key_works: Zhou et al. (2023), “Review of progress and challenges of key mechanical issues in high-field superconducting magnets,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1093/nsr/nwad001).

title: Persistent REBCO joints at full precision-magnet scale
open: Can superconducting joints between REBCO conductors be made to survive everything a full-scale, high-field persistent magnet demands of them — the full current, the field angle, thermal and electromagnetic cycling, and years of low drift — repeatably, with acceptable yield and repairability? Formally, the goal is a complete high-field persistent magnet in which every joint meets its current, field-angle, cycling, drift, yield, and repair requirements.
status: A persistent 400 MHz NMR prototype with HTS joints was demonstrated in 2021 (Yanagisawa et al. (2021), "Development of a persistent-mode NMR magnet with superconducting joints between high-temperature superconductors," https://doi.org/10.1088/1361-6668/ac2120; Takeda et al. (2025), "Temperature, magnetic field, and field angular dependence of critical current of REBCO intermediate grown superconducting joint," https://doi.org/10.1088/1361-6668/ae1eaa). Scaling joint performance to more demanding complete systems remains open.
solved_when: A complete high-field persistent magnet is built in which repeatable superconducting joints meet the stated current, field-angle, cycling, drift, yield, and repair requirements throughout.
why: Persistent joints free the magnet from its power supply and suppress long-term field drift, which is what precision applications such as NMR ultimately require.
key_works: Yanagisawa et al. (2021), “Development of a persistent-mode NMR magnet with superconducting joints between high-temperature superconductors,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1088/1361-6668/ac2120); Takeda et al. (2025), “Temperature, magnetic field, and field angular dependence of critical current of REBCO intermediate grown superconducting joint,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1088/1361-6668/ae1eaa).

title: Training-free full-size Nb3Sn magnets throughout service life
open: Can a full-size Nb3Sn magnet be built that reaches its design field without any training quenches and stays that way through every thermal and irradiation cycle of its service life, using support and impregnation methods that transfer across magnet designs?
status: Training in superconducting magnets has persisted for decades. A 2025 report by Barzi, “Elimination of training in Nb3Sn and NbTi superconducting magnets,” [NAPAC2025 contribution](https://indico.jacow.org/event/97/contributions/10539/), describes nearly eliminated training in specific undulators; however, full-size collider qualification remains a distinct challenge.
solved_when: A full-size Nb3Sn magnet demonstrates commissioning and retraining quench elimination — no training quenches initially and none after thermal and irradiation cycles — while retaining design field and mechanical integrity, with support and impregnation methods shown to be transferable to other magnets.
why: Removing training quenches cuts commissioning time and helium consumption and reduces the risk of magnet damage during bring-up.
key_works: Barzi (2025), “Elimination of training in Nb3Sn and NbTi superconducting magnets,” [NAPAC2025 contribution](https://indico.jacow.org/event/97/contributions/10539/).

title: Uniform overpressure processing of large Bi-2212 coils
open: Can a large, complex Bi-2212 winding be overpressure processed so that high current is achieved uniformly throughout the coil, while simultaneously controlling bubble formation, oxygen activity, dimensional changes, insulation compatibility, and temperature uniformity?
status: Overpressure processing enabled high-current round wire in 2014, as reported by Larbalestier et al. (2014), "Isotropic round-wire multifilament cuprate superconductor for generation of magnetic fields above 30 T" ([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/nmat3887)), and subsequent accelerator coils; however, large-coil production yield remains difficult.
solved_when: High superconducting current is reproduced throughout a large complex winding after overpressure processing, with bubbles controlled, oxygen activity managed, dimensional changes and insulation compatibility held within acceptable limits, and temperature uniformity maintained across the coil — achieving acceptable large-coil production yield.
why: It provides an isotropic round-wire high-temperature-superconductor route to powerful magnets, extending the 2014 demonstration from short samples and accelerator coils to reliable production-scale coils.
key_works: Larbalestier et al. (2014), “Isotropic round-wire multifilament cuprate superconductor for generation of magnetic fields above 30 T,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/nmat3887).

title: Rapid-ramping HTS magnets with acceptable total losses
open: Can a high-temperature superconducting magnet be ramped rapidly to high field while keeping its total losses — hysteretic, coupling, eddy-current, and refrigeration — within an acceptable budget? A successful design must also preserve field quality and remain protectable during fast ramping.
status: Large static HTS magnets and rotating-machine applications exist, but high static critical current does not establish efficient rapid-cycle operation. Coombs et al. (2024), "High-temperature superconductors and their large-scale applications," [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s44287-024-00112-y).
solved_when: A rapid-ramping HTS magnet demonstrates useful high-field ramp rates with total hysteretic, coupling, eddy-current, and refrigeration losses within budget, while retaining field quality and quench protection.
why: It would enable compact synchrotrons and responsive industrial magnets, applications that rapid-cycle HTS operation currently does not support efficiently.
key_works: Coombs et al. (2024), “High-temperature superconductors and their large-scale applications,” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s44287-024-00112-y).

title: Practical ultrahigh-field whole-body MRI magnets
open: Can a whole-body ultrahigh-field MRI magnet be built small, light, and simple enough to service that hospitals could actually install and run it, while keeping the bore, field homogeneity, stability, and fringe-field control that imaging demands?

why: It would carry ultrahigh-field imaging out of a handful of specialized installations into routine clinical and research settings.

title: High-duty-cycle nondestructive 100 T-class pulsed magnets
open: Can a nondestructive pulsed magnet sustain operation near 100 T at a high duty cycle — many pulses, long useful duration — without sacrificing fatigue life or degrading experimental conditions? Formally, the goal is to co-optimize pulse count and duration near 100 T while simultaneously extending coil fatigue life and reducing cooldown time, vibration, and measurement noise.
status: Nondestructive 100 T-class pulses have existed since 2012. Peak field, pulse duration, repetition rate, and coil life remain conflicting objectives, so no current design optimizes them jointly. Related engineering directions include long-lived pulsed-power switches and materials for extreme cyclic fatigue. A laboratory report from the National High Magnetic Field Laboratory (2021), "New Pulsed Magnet Reveals a New State of Matter in Kondo Insulator," illustrates current capabilities.
solved_when: A nondestructive 100 T-class pulsed magnet is demonstrated that simultaneously achieves high pulse repetition, long useful pulse duration, extended fatigue life, and reduced cooldown, vibration, and measurement noise relative to present designs.
why: It would make extreme-field phase diagrams and weak-signal measurements far more accessible, since longer and more frequent pulses give experiments more usable measurement time at fields near 100 T.
key_works: National High Magnetic Field Laboratory (2021), “New Pulsed Magnet Reveals a New State of Matter in Kondo Insulator,” [laboratory report](https://nationalmaglab.org/news-events/news/75-tesla-duplex-magnet-kondo-insulator/).

title: Sustainable procurement for specialty superconducting wire
open: How can we design purchasing, qualification, and funding mechanisms that keep specialized superconducting wire production, technical capability, supplier diversity, and research-scale access alive between major magnet projects? The goal is a durable stewardship and procurement model that survives the irregular demand cycles characteristic of the field.
status: A 2023 stakeholder report by Cooley, Amm, Hischier, Rotkoff, and Larbalestier (2023), "Business models to assure availability of advanced superconductors for the accelerator sector and promote stewardship of superconducting magnet technology for the US economy," [arXiv:2308.03808](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.03808), proposes stewardship models addressing irregular demand. Durable implementation and evaluation across project cycles remain open.
solved_when: A durable mechanism for purchasing, qualification, and funding is implemented and evaluated across project cycles, preserving specialized wire production, technical capability, supplier diversity, and research-scale access between major projects.
why: It prevents the loss of manufacturing knowledge and avoids future magnet bottlenecks when demand resumes.
key_works: Cooley, Amm, Hischier, Rotkoff, and Larbalestier (2023), “Business models to assure availability of advanced superconductors for the accelerator sector and promote stewardship of superconducting magnet technology for the US economy,” [arXiv:2308.03808](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.03808).
